# Volume 2 — VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

It was a day in September upon the hills of St. Brendan’s Island; an invigorating breeze blew from the ocean across the sand dunes; a lengthy red road wound amid woods and fields, at times curving around a bend of dense spruces, at times passing through a grove of youthful maples with vast, plume-like expanses of ferns beneath, at times descending into a depression where a stream emerged briefly from the trees before re-entering them, at times reclining in the unshaded sunlight amidst stripes of smoke-blue asters and golden-rod; the atmosphere vibrated with the chirping of countless crickets, those joyful small dependents of the summer slopes; a stout brown pony ambled down the route; a pair of girls sat behind him, brimful with the pure, invaluable happiness of vitality and youth.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0000 }

“Oh, this is a day left over from Eden, isn’t it, Isolde?” . . . and Nell sighed out of pure joy. “Magic fills the air. See the purple shade resting in the basin of the harvest valley, Isolde. And oh, do catch the scent of the dying fir! That aroma rises from the small sunny hollow where Mr. Eben Duckett has been chopping fence poles. To be alive on a day like this is bliss; but smelling dying fir is sheer heaven. Two thirds of that comes from Wordsworth and one third from Nell Harcourt. It hardly seems possible for dying fir to exist in heaven, does it? Yet I feel heaven would lack complete perfection if you failed to catch a breeze of dead fir while walking in its forests. Maybe the scent will exist there apart from death. Yes, I believe it will work that way. That delightful smell has to be the firs’ souls . . . and naturally heaven will consist only of souls.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0001 }

“Trees don’t possess souls,” practical Isolde remarked, “yet the aroma of dead fir is undeniably wonderful. I intend to craft a cushion and stuff it with needles from the firs. You ought to craft one as well, Nell.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0002 }

“I believe I will . . . and nap inside it. That would surely make me dream of being a woodnymph or a dryad. Right now, though, I am completely satisfied being the Brierley schoolteacher, Nell Harcourt, traveling along a road like this on a day so friendly and sweet.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0003 }

“The weather is delightful, yet our upcoming duty is far from pleasant,” Isolde let out a sigh. “What possessed you to volunteer for this street, Nell? Nearly every eccentric person in Brierley resides here, and people will likely view us as if we are soliciting handouts for our own benefit. Of all the streets, this is absolutely the most dreadful.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0004 }

“I selected it for that very reason. Naturally, Hugh and Gideon would have chosen this path had we requested them to do so. However, Isolde, as the person who originally proposed the B.V.I.S., I consider myself accountable for it, so it feels right that I should take on the most unpleasant tasks. My apologies to you for this; nevertheless, you are not required to utter a single word when we reach the difficult spots. The speaking will be handled entirely by me . . . According to Mrs. Sowerby, I am certainly capable of doing so. Mrs. Sowerby remains undecided about whether she should support our project. She leans toward favoring it whenever she recalls Mr. and Mrs. Wace’s endorsement; on the other hand, the American origins of village improvement societies serve as a point against it. Consequently, she wavers between both views, meaning Mrs. Sowerby will judge us favorably only if we succeed. Honora plans to compose an essay for our upcoming Improvement gathering, which I anticipate will be excellent, given how gifted her aunt is at writing and how likely such talent is inherited. Discovering that Mrs. Charlotte E. Varley was aunt to Honora provided me with an unforgettable excitement. It felt truly extraordinary that I held a friendship with the young woman whose aunt authored ‘Edgewood Days’ and ‘The Rosebud Garden.’”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0005 }

“Where is Mrs. Varley’s residence?”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0006 }

“In Toronto. Also, Honora mentions that she plans to travel to the Island for a visit next summer, and provided it can be managed, Honora intends to organize a way for us to meet her. That appears nearly too wonderful to actually happen—yet it gives you something nice to picture once you get into bed.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0007 }

An established reality was the Brierley Village Improvement Society. Serving as president was Hugh Carrow, with Gideon Duckett as vice-president, Nell Harcourt as secretary, and Isolde Pembroke as treasurer. At the residences of its members, the “Improvers,” a nickname given to them right away, were scheduled to gather every two weeks. Although it was acknowledged that accomplishing numerous enhancements this late in the year was unlikely, their intention was to organize the upcoming summer's efforts, gather and analyze suggestions, compose and recite essays, and, to quote Nell, “educate the public sentiment generally.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0008 }

Naturally, a degree of opposition existed, alongside a significant amount of mockery, which wounded the Improvers far more deeply. It was rumored that Mr. Elisha Duckett had remarked that calling the association the Courting Club would suit it better. Mrs. Hiram Mott announced that word had reached her that the Improvers intended to till every roadside and plant geraniums along them. A caution was issued by Mr. Levi Gammon to his neighbors, stating the Improvers would demand that all residents demolish their homes and construct new ones following society-sanctioned designs. A message was delivered from Mr. James Tranter expressing his desire for them to pleasantly flatten the church hill. Nell was informed by Eben Duckett of his hope that the Improvers might persuade old Josiah Mott to trim his beard. Mr. Lawrence Bell stated that he was willing to apply whitewash to his barns if that was required to satisfy them, but hanging lace curtains in the cowstable windows was where he drew the line. A question was posed by Mr. Major Tranter to Clifton Mott, a member of the Improvers who transported milk to the cheese factory in Delford, inquiring whether it was a fact that all residents would be required to hand-paint their milk-stands by the following summer and adorn them with embroidered centerpieces.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0009 }

Regardless of this . . . or maybe, given how human nature operates, on account of it . . . the Society courageously set to work on the sole upgrade they had any chance of accomplishing that autumn. During their second assembly, located in the Pembroke parlor, Oliver Mott proposed starting a collection of funds to put new shingles and paint on the hall; Julia Bell provided a second to the motion, though she felt uncomfortable and worried that her action was not quite proper for a lady. Hugh presented the motion to a vote, everyone voted in favor of it, and Nell soberly entered it into her minutes. Selecting a committee was the subsequent task, and Tibby Tulk, who was resolved to prevent Julia Bell from taking all the glory, daringly proposed that Miss Odette Pullen serve as the head of the designated committee. After this proposal was likewise properly seconded and passed, Odette repaid the favor when she named Tibby to the committee, together with Hugh, Nell, Isolde, and Gideon Duckett. The members of the committee selected their assigned paths during a confidential meeting. Nell and Isolde received their assignment for the Stonebridge road, Hugh and Gideon were designated for the Pale Sands road, and Odette and Tibby were selected for the Delford road.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0010 }

“Because,” Hugh clarified to Nell, while the pair traversed the Whispering Wood on their way home, “the Tulks reside entirely on that road, and they refuse to contribute a single cent unless a member of their own group solicits them.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0011 }

Nell and Isolde set off the following Saturday. Having driven to where the road ended, they worked their way back toward home, visiting the “Andrew girls” before anyone else.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0012 }

Isolde remarked, “If Catherine is by herself we might obtain something, but if Eliza is present we will not.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0013 }

Eliza was present . . . to a great degree . . . and possessed an appearance even more severe than she normally did. Miss Eliza belonged to that category of individuals who convey the feeling that existence is truly a valley of sorrow, and that grinning, not to mention laughing, constitutes a genuinely blameworthy misuse of nervous force. The Andrew sisters had been known as “girls” for a bit more than fifty years and appeared probable to continue as girls until the conclusion of their journey on earth. Catherine, according to rumor, had not completely abandoned hope, whereas Eliza, a pessimist from birth, had never possessed any. Their home was a tiny brown dwelling constructed in a sunlit spot carved out of Mark Andrew’s beech forest. Eliza grumbled that the heat was dreadful during summer, whereas Catherine was accustomed to remarking that it was delightfully warm during winter.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0014 }

Eliza was stitching together pieces of quilt, not out of any necessity, but purely to demonstrate her disapproval of the light, ornamental lace that Catherine was making with her hook. Eliza paid attention while wearing a scowl and Catherine while wearing a grin, as the young women made the purpose of their visit clear. Naturally, every time Catherine’s gaze met Eliza’s, she abandoned her grin out of remorseful embarrassment; nevertheless, it reappeared a short time later.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0015 }

“Were I possessed of funds to squander,” Eliza remarked sternly, “I would ignite them and perhaps enjoy the spectacle of a fire; however, I refuse to grant a single penny to that hall. The community gains nothing from it . . . it serves merely as a gathering spot for youth to misbehave when they ought to be sleeping in their beds at home.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0016 }

“Oh, Eliza, a bit of entertainment is necessary for youth,” Catherine objected.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0017 }

“The need for it escapes me. When we were young, Catherine Pullen, we did not go gallivanting to halls and such locations. With each passing day, this world deteriorates.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0018 }

“I believe the situation is improving,” declared Catherine with conviction.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0019 }

“You believe!” The deepest disdain was evident in Miss Eliza’s tone. “Whatever you believe holds no importance, Catherine Pullen. Facts remain facts.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0020 }

“Well, Eliza, I am always fond of viewing things positively.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0021 }

“There is no silver lining.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0022 }

“Oh, indeed there is,” exclaimed Nell, who was unable to quietly tolerate such heresy. “Why, there are so very many bright sides, Miss Pullen. It is truly a beautiful world.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0023 }

“You won’t hold it in such high regard once you’ve spent as much time in it as I have,” Miss Eliza replied testily, “nor will you display such eagerness to make it better. Isolde, how is your mother? Goodness gracious, she has certainly declined recently. She appears extremely exhausted. And Nell, how much time does Thirza have left until she anticipates becoming completely blind?”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0024 }

“Her eyes will not deteriorate further if she exercises extreme caution, according to the doctor,” Nell stammered.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0025 }

Eliza gave a negative shake of her head.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0026 }

“Medical men perpetually speak in that manner merely to maintain folks' spirits. Were I in her place, I would not possess great expectations. One ought to be ready for the most dreadful outcome.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0027 }

“Must we not prepare ourselves for the finest outcome as well?” Nell implored. “That is precisely as probable as the most terrible.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0028 }

“I have not found that to be true, and my fifty-seven years outweigh your sixteen,” Eliza shot back. “Are you leaving? Well, it is my hope that your new society can prevent Brierley from slipping any lower, though my expectations are small.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0029 }

Nell and Isolde gratefully disembarked, before departing as rapidly as the chubby pony was able to travel. When they made their way around the bend beneath the beech wood, a chubby person arrived running across Mr. Pullen’ pasture, gesturing at them with great excitement. The person was Catherine Pullen, and being so short of breath that speaking was nearly impossible for her, she nevertheless pushed two quarters into the hand of Nell.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0030 }

“This represents what I can offer toward the hall painting,” she panted. “Giving a dollar to you would be my preference, yet taking an additional sum out of my egg savings is something I dare not attempt, as Eliza would discover it if I were to do so. Your society holds a true interest for me, and my belief is that you will accomplish a great deal of good. My nature is that of an optimist. Living alongside Eliza leaves me no choice but to be one. Returning quickly is necessary before my absence is noticed by her . . . she believes I am busy feeding the hens. May you experience good fortune while canvassing, and refrain from feeling discouraged by Eliza's words. Better times are coming to the world . . . they truly are.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0031 }

Daniel Blair’s was the subsequent house.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0032 }

“At present, everything hinges on his wife being there or absent,” Isolde remarked, while they bounced down a track marked with deep ruts. “Should she be present, not one cent will come to us; all the town declares Dan Blair lacks the courage to get a haircut unless she allows it, and to speak mildly, her stinginess is beyond doubt. Her own explanation is that being just must precede being generous. However, according to Mrs. Sowerby, that 'preceding' distance is so great that she never achieves generosity whatsoever.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0033 }

During that evening, Thirza was told by Nell about what had happened to them at the Blair place.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0034 }

“After hitching the horse, we knocked on the kitchen door. No one answered, yet the door was unlocked, and someone could be heard in the pantry, carrying on terribly. Although we were unable to understand the words, Isolde claims she recognizes they were curses based on their tone. I am unable to think that of Mr. Blair, since he is constantly so silent and humble; however, he certainly had strong cause, because Thirza, when the unfortunate man arrived at the door, as red as a beet, with sweat running down his face, he was wearing a large gingham apron belonging to his wife. ‘I can’t get this durned thing off,’ he said, ‘for the strings are tied in a hard knot and I can’t bust ’em, so you’ll have to excuse me, ladies.’ We pleaded with him not to speak of it, then entered and took a seat. Mr. Blair also took a seat; he swiveled the apron around to his rear and rolled it up, yet he appeared so humiliated and anxious that I pitied him, and Isolde stated she worried we had visited at an awkward moment. ‘Oh, not at all,’ said Mr. Blair, attempting to grin . . . you are aware he is continually quite courteous . . . ‘I’m a little busy . . . getting ready to bake a cake as it were. My wife got a telegram today that her sister from Montreal is coming tonight and she’s gone to the train to meet her and left orders for me to make a cake for tea. She writ out the recipe and told me what to do but I’ve clean forgot half the directions already. And it says, ‘flavor according to taste.’ What does that mean? How can you tell? And what if my taste doesn’t happen to be other people’s taste? Would a tablespoon of vanilla be enough for a small layer cake?”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0035 }

“My sympathy for the unfortunate fellow grew deeper than ever. He appeared to be completely out of his element. Having heard tales of henpecked husbands, I now believed I was looking at one. I was on the verge of stating, ‘Mr. Blair, if you’ll give us a subscription for the hall I’ll mix up your cake for you.’ However, it abruptly occurred to me that driving such a hard bargain with a struggling fellow creature would not be very neighborly. Therefore, I volunteered to mix his cake without demanding anything in return. He eagerly accepted my proposal right away. He explained that although he was accustomed to baking his own bread prior to his marriage, he worried that cake exceeded his abilities, though he dreaded letting his wife down. After he retrieved a second apron for me, Isolde whipped the eggs while I combined the cake ingredients. Mr. Blair scurried around, fetching us the necessary items. Having completely forgotten he was still wearing his apron, it trailed behind him as he dashed about, causing Isolde to remark that the sight would be the death of her. He mentioned that baking the cake would pose no problem . . . he possessed experience with that part . . . and he subsequently requested our sheet and pledged four dollars. Thus, as you can tell, our efforts brought a reward. Nevertheless, had he withheld every penny, I would still maintain that assisting him constituted a genuinely Christian deed.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0036 }

The location where Theodore White resided served as the subsequent destination. Nell and Isolde were both visiting for the first time, and their familiarity with Mrs. Theodore was extremely minimal, as she rarely entertained guests. They debated in hushed tones whether to approach the rear entrance or the main entrance. During this quiet discussion, Mrs. Theodore emerged at the front entrance carrying a bundle of newspapers. In a calculated manner, she placed them individually upon the floor of the porch, the steps of the porch, and along the walkway until reaching the exact spot where her bewildered visitors stood.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0037 }

“Would you mind wiping your feet very thoroughly on the grass before stepping onto these papers?” she asked with concern. “I have only just finished sweeping the entire house, so I cannot tolerate any additional dust being brought inside. Ever since yesterday’s rain, the path has been extremely muddy.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0038 }

“Do not presume to laugh,” Nell cautioned softly while they stepped over the newsprint. “Furthermore, Isolde, I beg you to refrain from glancing my way, regardless of her words, lest I prove incapable of remaining serious.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0039 }

The documents spread throughout the entrance and went into a neat, immaculate parlor. Nell and Isolde seated themselves cautiously upon the closest chairs and detailed the reason for their visit. Mrs. White listened to them courteously, pausing the conversation a mere two times, first to drive away a daring fly, and second to gather a minute piece of grass that had dropped onto the rug from the dress of Nell. Nell experienced a miserable sense of guilt; nevertheless, Mrs. White pledged two dollars and handed over the cash immediately . . . “to prevent us from having to go back for it,” Isolde remarked after they escaped. Mrs. White had collected the newspapers prior to them unfastening their horse, and while they moved their vehicle out of the driveway, they observed her vigorously sweeping with a broom inside the entrance.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0040 }

“After what we just saw, I am convinced that the rumors about Mrs. Theodore White being the most orderly person in existence are true,” remarked Isolde, letting out her pent-up amusement the moment she could safely do so.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0041 }

“It makes me happy that no children were born to her,” Nell remarked with gravity. “Had there been any, their situation would have been terribly awful.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0042 }

During the visit to the Spencers’, Mrs. Isabella Tranter caused everyone distress by uttering a spiteful remark regarding every person in Brierley. Mr. Thomas Gammon declined to contribute any funds on the grounds that two decades earlier, when the hall was constructed, it was not erected upon the location he had advised. Mrs. Esther Bell, appearing perfectly healthy, spent thirty minutes describing each of her ailments in detail, and mournfully pledged fifty cents since she claimed she would not be alive to contribute when that time arrived the following year . . . rather, she expected to be buried in her grave.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0043 }

Their most unpleasant welcome, nevertheless, happened at Simon Fletcher’s. As they pulled into the yard, a pair of faces was seen by them looking out from the porch window. Yet despite the fact that they knocked and stood by with patience and persistence, not a soul answered the door. A pair of distinctly flustered and angry girls departed in their carriage from Simon Fletcher’s. Nell herself conceded that a sense of discouragement was starting to come over her. Nevertheless, the situation improved following that moment. A number of Mott properties were visited next, at which generous donations were secured by them, and from then until the conclusion they met with success, suffering merely a rare rejection. The final location they visited was at Robert Dickson’s near the pond bridge. They remained for tea at this house, even though home was quite close, to avoid the chance of angering Mrs. Dickson, who possessed the fame of being an extremely “touchy” lady.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0044 }

During the time they spent in that place, an visit was paid by elderly Mrs. James White.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0045 }

“I’ve just come back from Lorenzo’s,” she declared. “Right now, he’s the proudest man in Brierley. Guess what? A brand new boy is there . . . and following seven girls, I can assure you that’s quite an event.” Nell listened intently, and as they drove off she remarked.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0046 }

“My immediate destination is Lorenzo White’s place.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0047 }

“However, his residence is along the Pale Sands road, which takes us considerably off our route,” Isolde objected. “Gideon and Hugh are going to solicit his vote.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0048 }

“Next Saturday is when they are going around, which makes it far too late,” Nell stated with conviction. “By that point, the novelty will have vanished. Even though Lorenzo White is terribly stingy, he is willing to contribute to any cause right at this moment. Isolde, this golden chance cannot be allowed to pass.” Nell’s shrewdness was validated by the outcome. In the yard, Mr. White encountered them, radiating joy like the sun on an Easter morning. He offered his eager assent when Nell requested a contribution.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0049 }

“Without a doubt, without a doubt. Simply record my name for one dollar above the largest contribution you have received.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0050 }

“Five dollars is the amount . . . four was what Mr. Daniel Blair left,” Nell said, feeling a bit fearful. Lorenzo, however, did not shrink back.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0051 }

“Five it is . . . and the cash is right here on the spot. Now, my desire is for you to step inside the house. A sight worth taking in awaits in there . . . a thing that very few individuals have laid eyes on up to now. Simply step inside and give your verdict.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0052 }

“In the event that the infant lacks beauty, what shall be our response?” Isolde inquired in a fearful whisper while they trailed behind the enthusiastic Lorenzo into the residence.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0053 }

“Oh, something else pleasant will surely be said regarding it,” Nell remarked casually. “A baby always brings that out.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0054 }

The infant possessed beauty, nevertheless, and Mr. White considered the five dollars well spent for the genuine joy the chubby little arrival brought the girls. Yet that instance marked the single, ultimate, and solitary occasion on which Lorenzo White ever contributed to a cause.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0055 }

Exhausted though she felt, Nell exerted herself one last time that evening for the general good, stealing across the meadows to speak with Mr. Pettifer, who sat according to his habit on the veranda, smoking his pipe with Nutmeg at his side. Technically, his residence was situated on the Delford road; nevertheless, Odette and Tibby, who knew him only through dubious rumor, had anxiously pleaded with Nell to solicit his support.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0056 }

Mr. Pettifer, nevertheless, utterly declined to contribute a penny, and every one of Nell’s charms proved futile.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0057 }

“However, it was my impression that our society had your approval, Mr. Pettifer,” she lamented.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0058 }

“Indeed I do . . . indeed I do . . . yet my consent fails to reach as deep as my coin, Nell.”
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0059 }

“If I were to undergo just a couple more events like those I encountered today, I would become just as pessimistic as Miss Eliza Pullen,” Nell remarked to her image in the mirror of the east gable as she prepared for sleep.
{: #nw-v02-c06-p0060 }
